Science.title: Structural basis for regulating lipopolysaccharide transmembrane transport
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11129-8 Structures of the protein machinery in Gram-negative bacteria that transports lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from the cytoplasmic membrane to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane reveal how conformational changes in response to the presence of LPS promote its transport.

Science.title: International experience gives business leaders an edge, study finds
Science.summary: Business leaders with international experience play a significant role in shaping the success of their organizations and are often associated with stronger organizational performance, including higher growth, profitability and stock market performance, according to a new study published in the Journal of Management.

Science.title: Blend
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02864-z Identity crisis.

Science.title: Cryo-EM structure of a methanogen nitrogenase–PII protein supercomplex
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11116-z Cryo-electron microscopy of a nitrogenase supercomplex from a methane-producing archaeon reveals a mechanism in which PII proteins drive assembly of such structures to regulate nitrogenase activity in response to nitrogen availability.

Science.title: 'It looks like a chimera' — 168 million years ago, a strange platypus-like mammal relative lived in China alongside dinosaurs
Science.summary: A predatory mammal-like animal from the Jurassic seems to have characteristics of both a platypus and an otter.

Science.title: 'We stocked an RV as an emergency bugout vehicle': Readers share how prepared they are for a disaster
Science.summary: With extreme weather conditions becoming more frequent, having a disaster kit and other emergency plans can be beneficial. Live Science readers shared their thoughts about how prepared they are for these events. Do you agree with what they said?

Science.title: Nobel physics winner's pride at pioneering AI role
Science.summary: Francis Halzen, winner of the Nobel Prize in physics, spoke with pride on Wednesday about his early promotion of artificial intelligence in his research on neutrinos.

Science.title: OpenAI posts 700 maths preprints online: mathematicians are up in arms
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03196-8 The firm used unreleased models to tackle hundreds of high-profile problems.

Science.title: Genome accessibility reveals disease risk that gene expression misses
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03072-5 Most disease-associated genetic alterations do not affect the genes themselves, but instead change how strongly they are expressed, often by modifying genome accessibility. Gene expression and accessibility have now been analysed simultaneously in 10 million immune cells from 1,108 people, linking disease-associated changes in accessibility to gene expression.

Science.title: Retrofitted LLM can count the letter ‘i’s in ‘artificial intelligence’
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03059-2 Most LLMs cannot reliably evaluate text on the level of individual letters. A technique called byteification retrofits existing models to enable it.

Science.title: First global genome atlas reveals overlooked microscopic life in hundreds of lakes and reservoirs
Science.summary: Tiny single-celled organisms help keep lakes clear, but some can also contaminate the water. An international research team has analyzed DNA data from 362 lakes to create the first global genome atlas of these organisms. With the findings now published in Nature Communications, the new atlas lays the foundation for faster and more precise monitoring of lakes.

Science.title: First-in-kind data set reveals insights across the world's national and regional economies
Science.summary: The University of Virginia has published the Global Capitalism Index (GCI), a first-in-kind data set offering unprecedented insights into the globe's capitalism conditions in every country. Assembled from more than two hundred data sets across eight key pillars, the GCI's country-by-country scores offer an array of ways to understand capitalism around the world.

Science.title: Human lung organoid modelling of tissue-resident antiviral T cell responses
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11114-1 Lung organoids containing endogenous resident immune cells show that SARS-CoV-2 infection elicits protective, tissue-resident memory T cell responses, demonstrating local recall immunity and providing a platform for the study of human tissue-resident antiviral defence.

Science.title: Prehistoric global migration of vanishing gut microbes with humans
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11106-1 Microbial species disappearing from industrialized populations have evolved with humans over millennia and migrated worldwide with them—this may have consequences for human health.

Science.title: Dynamics of human cardiogenesis and its disruption in trisomy 21
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11125-y Single-cell and spatial multiomics are combined to define niches in the developing human heart, revealing pacemaker-cell organization, cardiomyocyte maturation and compaction, and developmental perturbations associated with trisomy 21.

Science.title: Chain reaction that begins when tumor suppression gene is switched off offers clues to how cancer develops
Science.summary: A tumor suppressor gene known as p53 is mutated in more than half of all cancers, but how it acts to prevent cancer formation is largely unknown. A study by UT Southwestern Medical Center researchers sheds light on this phenomenon by showing what happens when p53 becomes disabled, revealing the gene's diverse roles in maintaining healthy metabolic activity, repressing mobile genes called retrotransposons and preventing cells from adopting features of sperm and eggs.

Science.title: Giant tortoises outnumber people in Seychelles, with nearly 183,000 on Aldabra
Science.summary: A landmark survey of the world's largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has revealed that the once-endangered species is thriving and stable in the Seychelles.

Science.title: Can your brain grow new neurons? How researchers are solving a century-old puzzle
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03132-w Scientists have debated for decades whether the human brain sprouts new neurons throughout life. What would it mean if it could — and how much evidence is enough?

Science.title: 5-oxoETE links redox control of epithelial damage detection and resilience
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11121-2 The DHRS7–OXER1 pathway links oxidative stress to immunity and tissue resilience by modulating 5-oxoETE via NADP+–NADPH, activating OXER1 to recruit antimicrobial cells and induce NUDIX enzymes that protect epithelial redox integrity.

Science.title: Australia’s bush fires got worse after British colonization — this is why
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03184-y The suppression of Indigenous burning practices probably spurred the growth of flammable forests.

Science.title: Drug target could block brain inflammation linked to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s
Science.summary: Blocking a receptor called P2X7 significantly reduced inflammation in human brain tissue, revealing a potential new treatment strategy for neurological and psychiatric disorders. The discovery could help researchers repurpose existing drugs for conditions including traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, depression, and schizophrenia.

Science.title: NASA’s Webb finds signs of Mars-sized worlds smashing together
Science.summary: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope is giving astronomers a glimpse of the kinds of violent collisions that may have shaped our own solar system, including the giant impact thought to have created the Moon. By studying 21 rare “extreme debris disks” around young stars, researchers found that their dust can reveal the scale and intensity of planetary collisions.

Science.title: Superbug P. aeruginosa uses two protein plugs to seal channels against antibiotics
Science.summary: A joint research team has identified a new mechanism underlying antibiotic resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a major multidrug-resistant "superbug." The discovery provides important clues for the development of new treatments for multidrug-resistant bacterial infections. The findings are published in the journal Nature Communications.

Science.title: Hawaiian hot spot study uncovers evidence of true polar wander
Science.summary: On Earth, everything is moving. The planet spins, the tectonic plates shift and the spin axis wobbles, as do the magnetic poles, which makes determining how things move a rather tricky proposition. For Rice University's Richard Gordon, this problem came up when he was trying to understand the history of the Hawaiian hot spot, the deep-mantle source of the volcanism that created the Hawaiian–Emperor chain of islands and underwater volcanoes.

Science.title: Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03189-7 Intestinal bacterium secretes a molecule that reduces cholesterol production, according to a mouse study.

Science.title: Offshore wind turbine foundations may cool ocean surface by mixing seawater
Science.summary: New research within the PELAgIO ECOWind project has revealed how offshore wind farms can influence ocean temperatures and mixing, and why their effects depend on local conditions.

Science.title: Scientists discover the genetic secrets that may have helped Jonathan the tortoise live to 194 years old
Science.summary: DNA samples from Jonathan the 194-year-old tortoise reveal gene variants and epigenetic changes that could contribute to his remarkable lifespan.

Science.title: Alveolar stem cells transdifferentiate to drive bronchiolar regeneration
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11127-w Identification of a cross-compartmental cellular mechanism for bronchiolar epithelial repair informs therapeutic strategies for airway injury.

Science.title: Ultrashort laser pulses let new microscope map electron interactions across thin materials
Science.summary: A new type of advanced microscope (wide-field coherent multidimensional microscopy) has been developed. It uses a carefully designed sequence of ultrashort light pulses to study the behavior of high-tech materials, with potential practical applications in the study of innovative materials such as those used to build solar panels. Science.title: Gut microbes that trace ancient human journeys
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02969-5 The Indigenous African Hadza and South American Tsimane share gut microorganisms that shed light on human dispersals and microbial losses in industrialized societies.

Science.title: Gut microbes followed migrating humans across continents, new study suggests
Science.summary: New research looks at the surprising similarities in the gut microbiomes of hunter-gathers in Tanzania and horticulturalists in Bolivia, and asks: What role do these bacteria play in human health?

Science.title: How Spain's torrential rainstorms put sewage into its rivers and seas
Science.summary: After heavy rain, Spanish cities often awaken to refreshed air and clean streets, while the rainwater itself vanishes into storm drains along with everything it swept away. Underground, however, a very different story unfolds.

Science.title: 'Completely unexpected': Astronomers spy never-before-seen 'phoenix planet' rising from the ashes of a dead star
Science.summary: Astronomers have spotted a rare "second-generation" exoplanet closely orbiting the nearby white dwarf HS 0209+0832. An unusual mixture of heavy elements inside this zombie star suggests that "this system has given birth to a new world using the foundations of the old one."

Science.title: Snowball Earth's iron deposits may have formed through microbes living without sunlight
Science.summary: Iron is one of the most abundant metals on Earth's surface, yet how such massive iron ore deposits formed throughout geological history has long remained a mystery. The prevailing theory has been that ancient photosynthetic bacteria oxidized iron, causing it to precipitate and accumulate in the oceans.

Science.title: An early predecessor to mammals could swim, suckle and swallow
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03069-0 A fossil of an early ancestor of mammals from the Jurassic period reveals a mammal-like throat passage (pharynx) and throat bones (hyoids). It fills a gap in our knowledge about throat features in the animals from which modern mammals evolved their ability to swallow as adults and suckle milk as babies.

Science.title: Overcoming key challenges in the evolutionary transition to multicellularity
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11038-w This Review synthesizes an evolutionary framework for understanding the key stages, challenges and microevolutionary processes through which single cells evolve into functionally integrated multicellular organisms.

Science.title: Eight-year analysis reveals how sunlight and nutrients shape sustainable urban farming
Science.summary: Factors such as sunlight and stage-specific nutrient application determine crop success in urban agriculture, far beyond fixed recipes or miracle solutions. The findings are published in the journal Agronomy for Sustainable Development.

Science.title: Earth’s center is moving, and NASA just measured it
Science.summary: Earth’s center of mass is constantly on the move, shifting by a few millimeters as enormous amounts of water, ice, and even air migrate around the planet with the seasons. NASA scientists have developed a more precise way to track these tiny swings using laser-ranging satellites, GPS data, and measurements of how water and ice deform Earth’s crust.

Science.title: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
Science.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has found strong evidence that the rocky lava world HD 3167 b has an atmosphere, despite circling its star every 24 hours under extreme heat. The surprising discovery could help scientists understand how rocky planets retain atmospheres and what the young, molten Earth may once have looked like.

Science.title: A split attractor design for rapidly writing a navigational goal
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11144-9 The recurrent h∆K–PFG neural circuit generates persistent heading memories through slow excitation, fast inhibition and a disinhibitory gate, where disinhibition controls the functional coupling of the network to rapidly transition between measurement and memory.

Science.title: A Jurassic mammaliaform swimmer and transformation of the mammalian pharynx
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11107-0 A swimming and water-foraging mammaliaform, Megacauda sungei gen. et sp. nov., had a lifestyle analogous to the extant platypus, and was capable of mammal-like swallowing and suckling.

Science.title: Archaeologists discover a child's skull built into the floor of a 2,500-year-old Scandinavian house
Science.summary: A study of nearly 200 individuals buried in domestic contexts in ancient and Viking Age Scandinavia has revealed unusually high levels of violence.

Science.title: Survey finds K-12 educators self-censor to avoid controversy over book selections
Science.summary: Elementary school teachers often put such care into creating their classroom libraries: shelving multiple copies of each book, stringing lights around them to set the mood, situating beanbag chairs and magic carpet squares strategically to encourage students to settle in.

Science.title: A 7-eV bandgap semiconductor based on silicon-doped α-(Al x Ga 1− x ) 2 O 3
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11085-3 Suboxide molecular-beam epitaxy is used to grow silicon-doped α-(AlxGa1−x)2O3 films with bandgaps exceeding 7.0 eV, enabling the fabrication of a Schottky diode and a field-effect transistor with colossal-bandgap channels.

Science.title: Spatially deterministic nucleation of 2D semiconductors by etching flux
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11095-1 Etching-flux-mediated single-centred nucleation of two-dimensional semiconductors is used to deterministically localize a single nucleation event, expanding semiconductor deposition from controlling where materials grow to controlling where and how crystals can begin to form.

Science.title: Animals may have evolved 200 million years earlier than we thought
Science.summary: New research suggests animals could have evolved as early as 800 to 700 million years ago, roughly 200 million years earlier than some previous estimates. If so, the first animals may have lived before or during Snowball Earth, leaving behind little trace because their soft bodies were rarely preserved.

Science.title: From jargon to impact: Teaching undergraduates the art of public communication
Science.summary: Articles published in The Conversation go well beyond academics writing for a general audience—they can also serve as valuable content for educators to use in the classroom.

Science.title: Tiny plasma-grown particles enable easier magnetization reversal in materials for high-frequency electronics
Science.summary: Researchers at South China University of Technology, in collaboration with the Dongguan Institute of Materials Science and Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, have developed a novel supranano multi-precipitate microstructure in amorphous soft magnetic composites using Ar/O₂ plasma treatment. By facilitating magnetic-moment reversal, this approach significantly reduced coercivity while maintaining excellent overall performance.

Science.title: Acoustic experiments confirm topology can persist at gapless critical points
Science.summary: Two studies on critical topology have recently been published in the journal Nature. These studies were led by the teams of Prof. Baile Zhang at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, and Prof. Jianhua Jiang at the University of Science and Technology of China, respectively. Prof. Xue-Jia Yu from the School of Physics at the Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo (EIT), served as a co-corresponding author on both papers and provided key theoretical guidance in the related experimental collaborations.

Science.title: Retrofitting language models to operate over bytes
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11111-4 Byteification is a general method for retrofitting large language models to operate over bytes such that they approach the capabilities of subword-based systems and may be better for scientific data.

Science.title: Semiconductors pushed into insulator territory
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02968-6 A material that was previously assumed to be an electrical insulator has been shown to be a semiconductor, with potential uses in electronics and optics.

Science.title: A gut microbial odd-chain fatty acid alleviates atherosclerosis in mice
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11142-x The administration of Bacteroides uniformis in mice can mitigate atherosclerosis via pentadecanoic acid, which directly inhibits HMG-CoA reductase to promote hepatic cholesterol clearance.

Science.title: 'Self-blinking dyes' simplify nanoscale imaging without sacrificing precision
Science.summary: Nanobodies are extremely small antibody fragments that bind to specific molecules. When nanobodies are labeled with dyes, they can be used as probes to enhance super-resolution microscopy. However, conventional blinking dyes often perform poorly when attached to nanobodies, limiting their practical advantages. An international research team led by the University of Göttingen and the University Medical Center Göttingen (UMG) has now shown that self-blinking dyes—which can switch between bright and dark states on their own—bypass this limitation.

Science.title: Tiny photosynthetic organisms help transport carbon to the depths of the Baltic Sea
Science.summary: Tiny photosynthetic organisms in the Baltic Sea can contribute substantially to the transport of carbon from surface waters to deeper parts of the sea. A new study from the Department of Ecology, Environment and Plant Sciences at Stockholm University shows that their ability to form colonies and aggregates is an important factor determining how much of their biomass sinks.

Science.title: 'Sexy Mantis,' obscene orangutan and prancing sparrowhawk feature in 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards
Science.summary: The Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards has unveiled its finalists for 2026, so let's all have a good laugh at nature.

Science.title: Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
Science.summary: Giving zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule appears to bring out more natural behavior. The lions spent nearly three times longer feeding, engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food, and rested more heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.

Science.title: RNA catalysis emerges from dynamic structural ensembles
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11140-z RNase P RNA forms shifting active and inactive conformers whose catalytic activity depends on Mg2+-driven tertiary-interaction dynamics, which are modulated by binding of accessory proteins.

Science.title: Experimental observation of critical topology
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11099-x Experimental evidence indicating that critical gapless topological states can be characterized by the entanglement spectrum and wavefunctions is presented, demonstrating persistence of topology at phase boundaries and extension to higher-dimensional systems.

Science.title: Mechanism of spliceosome termination
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11101-6 A coordinated sequence of RNA helicases and associated factors dismantles normal and defective spliceosome complexes to enable intron degradation and ensure accurate gene expression.

Science.title: A chiral superlattice route to spin-split topological antiferromagnetism
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11073-7 A chiral superlattice in collinear antiferromagnetic UOTe generates large Berry curvature and spin-polarized currents, enabling anomalous Hall effects and advancing chiral quantum materials for spintronics.

Science.title: Undergraduate student may have solved puzzle regarding isolated galaxies that have stopped producing stars
Science.summary: An undergraduate astrophysics student at UC Berkeley has found three unusual galaxies—cataloged as Shapiro Dwarf Galaxies I, II and III. Each galaxy is far from other galaxies and has stopped making stars, a combination that is extremely rare. The discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal, provides compelling observational evidence of a long-held astronomical theory.

Science.title: How we ditched presentations and embraced silence in our lab meetings
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02836-3 Swapping to a system in which lab members read memos quietly before team discussions helped to create an open culture.

Science.title: New approach to plant stress studies could yield hardier crops and medical insights
Science.summary: At the University of Missouri, plant scientist Ron Mittler is rewriting the playbook for how scientists study life by asking what happens when living organisms face multiple stresses at once.

Science.title: The Draconids, an unpredictable shower that can bring hundreds of meteors per minute, has begun
Science.summary: Peaking on Oct. 8-9, the unpredictable Draconid meteor shower is one of the few that's best seen just after dark. Could it produce another meteor storm?

Science.title: A new way to fight gum disease without wiping out good bacteria
Science.summary: Scientists discovered that disrupting the chemical messages bacteria use to communicate can push dental plaque toward a healthier microbial balance. The approach could lead to new treatments for gum disease that control harmful bacteria without destroying beneficial species.

Science.title: Observation of critical topological phase transition
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11067-5 Using an acoustic metamaterial platform, a critical topological phase transition is experimentally demonstrated establishing a hierarchical phase transition organization, in which topology shapes criticality beyond the conventional Landau–Ginzburg paradigm and standard topological phase transitions.

Science.title: Roboticists showcase tiny, frog-like robot that can hop across wet surfaces and swim
Science.summary: A palm-sized robot inspired by frogs uses snapping rods to jump, swim and navigate an obstacle course.

Science.title: Physicists just found the ‘ghost’ of superconductivity
Science.summary: Physicists have found striking evidence for an unusual form of superconducting behavior in uranium ditelluride, where electron pairs organize into rippling patterns called pair density waves. Even more surprisingly, these patterns appear to survive after ordinary superconductivity disappears, suggesting that the electron pairs responsible for superconductivity may begin forming before the material actually becomes superconducting.

Science.title: Humans may not be as hardwired for violence as we thought
Science.summary: A study comparing 100 primate species, including humans, suggests that everyday aggression and lethal violence did not evolve as part of the same simple behavioral spectrum. Species that frequently fight or show mild aggression are not necessarily more likely to kill rivals, while extreme acts such as infanticide and lethal attacks appear to follow their own evolutionary patterns.

Science.title: 1,000-mile-long cloud that forms and vanishes on Mars every day obeys 'exotic physics' never seen on Earth
Science.summary: New simulations suggest that the perplexing Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC) repeatedly emerges in the Red Planet's skies thanks to a never-before-seen meteorological process.

Science.title: Earth is in the firing line of a strange new type of cosmic object, astronomers say
Science.summary: Astronomers may have discovered the first known microblazar, a long-theorized object firing a powerful beam of particles directly at Earth.

Science.title: ‘When prevention disappears, infections rise’: can the world still end AIDS?
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03127-7 The United Nations’ deadline for eliminating HIV/AIDS as a public-health threat is unlikely to be met. But medical, political and social advances have raised hopes that longer-term success is still possible.

Science.title: What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?
Science.summary: Cannabinoids may intensify anxiety by removing a natural brake on specific neurons in the brain’s fear center, particularly during stressful situations. In mice, shutting down those neurons sharply reduced cannabinoid-related anxious behavior.

Science.title: How to control where semiconductor crystals start growing
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02934-2 Semiconductor crystals grow from tiny nuclei, but the position of these nuclei is difficult to control precisely and can affect the crystal’s properties. An approach using ‘etching flux’ has now been developed that constrains the position at which a nucleus forms, enabling spatially programmable growth of large single crystals of semiconducting material.
